summary: RFC 8955 requires the originator of a BGP Flow Specification to match the originator of the best-match unicast route for the destination prefix, which limits where it can be originated. This document updates that validation so a Flow Specification can be originated from anywhere within the autonomous system, for example by a centralized controller.

eli5.summary: A rule about who can post traffic filters was too strict. This document loosens it so a central helper inside the same network can post them too.

subtitle: A small change to BGP Flow Specification validation so a central controller inside your own network can originate filters.

tldr.problem: RFC 8955 only accepts a BGP Flow Specification if its originator matches the originator of the best-match unicast route for the destination prefix. That rules out a centralized route controller in the same domain that is not in the forwarding path, and it also blocks Flow Specifications from route servers.
tldr.mechanism: The validation step gets a second way to pass: a Flow Specification whose AS_PATH is empty or holds only an AS_CONFED_SEQUENCE segment was originated inside the Local Domain. The eBGP AS_PATH rule is changed to compare the left-most AS with that of the best-match unicast route.
tldr.outcome: Operators can distribute intra-domain filtering from a central controller and can exchange Flow Specifications at Internet exchanges with route servers. Security stays about the same as BGP unicast routing, with some weakening when the peer is a route server.

today: RFC 9117 is a Proposed Standard from August 2021 that updates RFC 8955. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 8955 defines BGP NLRI that carries traffic Flow Specifications, which let BGP speakers distribute traffic filtering rules. The main aim is to let downstream autonomous systems tell upstream ones to filter traffic closer to the source, so the upstream networks do not carry traffic only to have it discarded.

Before a Flow Specification is considered feasible and installed in the Adj-RIB-In, it must pass validity checks. This document changes two of those checks. It does not change the Flow Specification format itself.
sections.eli5: Imagine a neighborhood where people can post notes saying which kind of mail to stop at the gate. This document changes who is allowed to post those notes.

sections.title: Terms Used in the Document
sections.content:
Three terms are defined. The Local Domain is the local AS or the local confederation of ASes. eBGP means BGP peering to a router not within the Local Domain. iBGP means classic iBGP plus any eBGP peering with a router in the same confederation; in short, any peering that is not eBGP as defined here.

The document uses the key words MUST, SHOULD and MAY as described in BCP 14 (RFC 2119 and RFC 8174).
sections.eli5: The 'Local Domain' is your own street. Friends on your street are iBGP peers, and anyone from another street is an eBGP peer.

sections.title: Why the Old Rule Gets in the Way
sections.content:
Step (b) of the validation in Section 6 of RFC 8955 assumes the Flow Specification travels the same path as the longest-match unicast route for the destination prefix inside it. For inter-domain filtering this works: at the egress border routers the Flow Specification originator matches the eBGP neighbor that advertised the best unicast route, and upstream routers see the matching egress iBGP border router.

Operators, however, often run a Security Operations Center and want to originate intra-AS Flow Specifications from a central BGP route controller that is not in the data forwarding plane. With the old rule, the controller would be seen as the originator, which never matches the border router that advertised the unicast route. The only workaround is to have each border router act as a de facto route controller, which is operationally cumbersome with many border routers and complex BGP policies.

The modification cannot be used for inter-domain coordination of traffic filtering. Its purpose is to make distributing intra-domain filtering policies simple, standard and scalable. Operators can then direct border routers to drop traffic or forward it to a pipe-cleaning location.
sections.eli5: The old rule said only the guard standing at the right gate could post the note. But the boss in the office could not, even though the boss knows best. This change lets the boss post the note.

sections.title: Revised Route Feasibility Check
sections.content:
Step (b) now says that one of two conditions MUST hold. Condition b.1 is the old one: the originator of the Flow Specification matches the originator of the best-match unicast route (the one with the longest prefix covering the destination prefix in the Flow Specification).

Condition b.2 is new: the AS_PATH of the Flow Specification is empty or contains only an AS_CONFED_SEQUENCE segment. Such a path shows the Flow Specification was originated inside the Local Domain, so a peer outside the forwarding path may originate it.

  • b.2 SHOULD be enabled by default.
  • b.2 MAY be disabled by explicit configuration on a BGP speaker, for example when the operator knows no Flow Specification will be originated inside the Local Domain.
  • By policy, a given non-empty AS_PATH MAY also be permitted, for example one with only an AS_SEQUENCE of ASes known to be in the same administrative domain.
sections.eli5: There are now two ways to get your note accepted: the guard at the right gate posts it, or someone from inside your own street posts it.

sections.title: Revised AS_PATH Validation for eBGP
sections.content:
RFC 8955 required that the AS_PATH of a Flow Specification received over eBGP has the neighboring AS in the left-most position. That blocks Internet exchanges with BGP route servers, which by design do not insert their own AS number into the AS_PATH (Section 2.2.2.1 of RFC 7947).

The new rule: the AS in the left-most position of the AS_PATH of an eBGP-received Flow Specification MUST match the AS in the left-most position of the AS_PATH of the best-match unicast route. The left-most AS means the AS that was last added to an AS_SEQUENCE.

The old check stays optional under Section 6.3 of RFC 4271, and a speaker may still enforce it. If the peer is not a route server, enforcing it gives security equivalent to RFC 8955. The RFC notes that not checking the full AS_PATH lets a rogue or misconfigured AS originate undesired Flow Specifications, a threat already present in RFC 8955 and out of scope here. Using the new rule for peers in the same Local Domain is also out of scope.
sections.eli5: A meeting-place helper passes notes along without signing them. So instead of checking the helper, the rule checks that the note's first signer matches the first signer on the matching delivery route.

sections.title: Topology Considerations
sections.content:
The originator in RFC 8955 is the ORIGINATOR_ID attribute or, if absent, the transport address of the peer the update came from. In the latter case the network should have a congruent topology, meaning the Flow Specification and its best-match unicast route are learned from the same peer. That fails, for example, if some peers negotiated only one Address Family or each Address Family peering has different policies.

Two examples of failure under the old rule: two BGP speakers with separate iBGP sessions for unicast and for Flow Specification and no ORIGINATOR_ID (such as a route reflector receiving from its clients), and a confederation where ORIGINATOR_ID is not advertised across local ASes and the two routes arrive from different peers Y1 and Y2.

With condition b.2, such non-congruent topologies work when the Flow Specification is originated in the Local Domain, because its AS_PATH is empty or has only an AS_CONFED_SEQUENCE. Flow Specifications from a different Local Domain still need a congruent topology.
sections.eli5: If the note and the delivery route come to you through different doors, the old rule gets confused. The new rule lets notes from your own street through anyway.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security properties stay essentially equivalent to BGP unicast routing, apart from the exceptions the RFC lists. The considerations in RFC 8955 still apply, and the changes in Section 4.1 do not affect validation of eBGP-learned routes.

Making the AS_PATH check optional again for the Flow Specification family can add risk with route servers. A speaker in AS X peering with a route server could advertise a rogue Flow Specification whose first AS is Y, where Y is also the first AS of the best-match unicast route. A speaker in AS Z validates it when the route server passes it on. This risk cannot be prevented for a route server peer. If the peer is known not to be a route server, the optional rule SHOULD be enforced, on unicast or Flow Specification routes. With no conclusive indication, it SHOULD NOT be enforced.

BGP updates from iBGP peers are considered trusted, so the intra-domain originator check is not required. That trust is not absolute, and a rogue iBGP speaker could now send a bad Flow Specification. The RFC argues that making intra-domain origination feasible makes the network overall more secure.
sections.eli5: Trusting your own street is mostly fine, but one bad neighbor could now post a fake note. The shared meeting place is riskier, so check the sender when you can.
